avis:
A Different POV on Westeros - AKOTSK is the latest adaptation of George R. R. Martin's works. It distinguishes itself from its predecessors with its much lighter atmosphere, humor, and jovial characters guided by honor and good intentions. We are indeed far from the heavy and sinister Shakespearean tragedies of HOTD and GOT.

Here, the sense of danger associated with Westeros is replaced by a tale of bravery and heroism, where a young hedge knight wishes to participate in a tournament to honor the memory of his deceased mentor. In his quest, he will be aided by a young squire, and it is the relationship between these two characters that initially creates the magic of the series. The story is captivating, and the music and sets succeed wonderfully in immersing us in this fantasy world.

According to some, compared to GOT and HOTD, AKOTSK is the best adaptation of the three, or at least definitely superior to HOTD. That's their prerogative, but it's clearly exaggerated! First, the total runtime of the season is barely equivalent to three episodes of GOT/HOTD. It follows a single story that takes place over just a few days and in the same location, with a very limited number of characters. Obviously, this is much easier to adapt than the dozens of complex plots that make up George R. R. Martin's main saga. The writing is decent, but the characters don't have a lot to say, so it's nothing like the intellectual prowess of Tyrion, Tywin, or Petyr Baelish.

As for HOTD, I can understand that the second season disappointed many, myself included, but some of those who criticize it today 'kinda forgot' how they once praised the talent of Paddy Considine as Viserys, Matt Smith as Daemon, and Rhys Ifans as Otto Hightower. Those who are swooning over AKOTSK for its 'powerful emotions' kinda forgot all those classic scenes like a dying Viserys taking place on the throne with the help of his brother, or young Aemond claiming Vhagar, not to mention all those epic moments from GOT such as Baelor, the outcome of the Mountain vs The Viper, or the first time we see the dragons in the last scene of season one. There is not a single moment in AKOTSK that made me feel anything close to that.

I would also argue that the episode In the Name of the Mother ranks among the best in the franchise, but certainly not with the early seasons of GOT, otherwise you have to admit that Dunk would have died at the end of the battle, considering that Ned never recovered from his leg injury. In this sense, the Trial of Seven is more comparable to the nonsense of BOTB and Jon Snow's plot armor, seeing that despite all his injuries, Dunk gets away with only a black eye. (Someone below lists all the hits Dunk takes during the fight; it's very revealing!) So yes, AKOTSK has a different and refreshing approach. It's a cute little story of chivalry, bravery, and honor like they don't make anymore. It's told in a simple way without the oppressive and dramatic aspects of GOT/HOTD, and it's overflowing with good feelings. It's also perfectly understandable that some fans appreciate that the story focuses on a single plot rather than scattering across dozens of more or less successful subplots like the later seasons of GOT. But I'm still going to wait and see a few seasons (and the third season of HOTD) before placing AKOTSK above the other two and deliberating on its place in history.

Why it deserves a 10/10 - In just a few minutes and across only a handful of episodes, the show managed to connect its events in a remarkably smooth and intelligent way. The pacing felt efficient without being rushed, allowing the story to unfold naturally while still keeping me fully engaged. Every scene seemed to serve a purpose, and the transitions between events were handled with clarity and precision. It's rare to see a series achieve this level of coherence so quickly, especially when dealing with complex storylines.

One of the most striking aspects was the cinematography. The visual presentation was truly exceptional, with carefully composed shots that enhanced both the mood and the storytelling. Lighting, camera angles, and scene composition were all used effectively to create a cinematic experience rather than just a typical TV show. At times, it felt like watching a high-quality film rather than a series, which added significantly to the overall impact.

The attention to detail in costumes and dialogue also stood out. The way the actors dressed reflected their characters and the world they lived in, adding authenticity and depth. Their manner of speaking was equally compelling, capturing the tone and style of the setting while still feeling natural and engaging. These elements helped bring the story to life and made it easier to become immersed in the narrative.

Overall, the combination of strong storytelling, outstanding visuals, and thoughtful character presentation made the experience highly enjoyable. It's clear that a lot of effort went into crafting every aspect of the show. For that, I can only say-thank you, Game of Thrones, for delivering such a memorable and well-executed piece of television.

avis:
It's not the game, It's Westeros - This is not Game of Thrones. This is Westeros, and for at least the first two episodes, it is glorious.

If you are looking for political intrigue, palace conspiracies, debates over military strategy, or mythical creatures roaming the land, you will not find them here. This is Westeros at peace, and for the most part, that is where it will remain. The only dragons are stitched onto banners. The direwolves remain north of the Wall. The Children of the Forest and the giants exist only in stories, and the realm is secure under the rule of the dynasty that created it.

The world is not changing. It is not on the brink of upheaval. That is not what this story is about.

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is about a man trying to remain good in that world, which turns out to present its own challenges, different from those faced when the wheel of power spins, offering the ladder of chaos to anyone willing to climb it. When ambition is quiet and history is not being written in blood, morality is no longer a weapon. It is a choice.

The adventures Ser Duncan the Tall and Egg stumble into will not reshape the fate of great houses or alter the course of history. Familiar names and ancient families appear mostly as brief cameos, there to ground the timeline and reward longtime fans rather than drive the plot. Instead, the story introduces us to the minor lords, the hedge knights, and the smallfolk who make up the overwhelming majority of the realm.

In doing so, it expands Westeros in a way that makes it feel lived in and real, something any fan of world-building or Game of Thrones lore should appreciate. And for those less invested in those, what you are really being offered is the Don Quixote of Westeros.

At its heart, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is about remaining good in a world that makes it all too easy to go bad. Dunk is not especially clever. He is not the best fighter. He is not smooth, calculating, or secretly destined to save the world. He is a regular man, raised to believe in a code, who stubbornly continues to live by it.

When the world darkens and tempts him to abandon that code, Egg is there to remind him of who he is, and more importantly, who he wants to be. Duncan's responsibility to teach another what it means to be a true knight, to impart honor, integrity, compassion, and justice to a boy who admires him, prevents the darkness from consuming the light within him.

It is a refreshing story that manages to feel, at the same time, timeless and timely. This series may not be the most exciting or the most complex Westeros has to offer, but if the remaining episodes are as strong as the first two, it will be one of the most beloved.

avis:
A lotus in the middle of a swamp - It's good to see the franchise return to the rawness and unapologetic edge that made Game of Thrones compelling in the first place. Going in, I was half-expecting the familiar "modern checklist" approach that can feel bolted on and distracting, but it never really showed up here-thankfully. Instead, the series leans into the kind of grounded, morally messy storytelling that suits this world: harsh consequences, blunt honesty, and a tone that doesn't flinch.

What I appreciated most is that the show seems more interested in character and atmosphere than in signalling. It trusts the setting to do the heavy lifting-political tension, personal ambition, and the ever-present sense that violence isn't a spectacle, it's a reality people live with. That restraint makes the drama land harder, and it helps the series feel closer in spirit to the early seasons of Thrones.

If the next seasons keep that same commitment-prioritising coherent world-building, believable motivations, and stakes that actually matter-this could become one of HBO's strongest returns to Westeros. For now, I genuinely enjoyed it, and I'm optimistic... as long as it stays true to the tone and instincts that made the original so gripping.

avis:
A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is an elite addition to the Game of Thrones universe - My wife and I finished the six-episode A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (2026) on MAX. The storyline follows a knight searching for purpose. He meets a young man and reluctantly takes him on as a squire. As the story unfolds, we learn about the troubled knight's past and upbringing while watching him try to carve out a meaningful role within the Seven Kingdoms-but it won't come easy. Fortunately, his squire proves to be far more useful than he ever anticipated.

The series was created by Ira Parker (House of the Dragon) and stars Peter Claffey (Small Things Like These), Dexter Sol Ansell (The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes), Tanzyn Crawford (Tiny Beautiful Things), and Daniel Ings (The Gentlemen).

I adored about 90% of this series. I loved how it simplifies the story within the Game of Thrones universe. The perspective is largely confined to one point of view, focusing on a single character. That's a refreshing change from the sprawling cast of characters and multiple kingdoms in Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon. Centering the narrative on one knight and his encounters within this world felt intimate and grounded-and it really worked.

The writing is strong throughout. The mindset, experience, and outlook of the two main characters are both fascinating and entertaining. The dialogue is clever and quick, and it's impossible not to like Egg. He keeps things grounded and balanced while serving as the emotional glue of the journey. The acting is elite, and the production value is top tier-easily on par with any prestige historical fantasy series. The attire, props, and settings fully immerse you in the world. The action scenes-especially in Episode 5-are magnificent, with the final battle standing out as a highlight.

The last episode let me down a bit. It felt somewhat slow and slightly disappointing overall, though I did enjoy the final five to ten minutes and the direction it sets up for the next season.

In conclusion, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is an elite addition to the Game of Thrones universe. I'd score it an 8.5-9/10 and highly recommend it.

Simply brilliant - Like the title says, this is brilliant.

If you really enjoyed the early seasons of Game of Thrones, then this is essential viewing.

Stripped of all the complicated politics, huge battles and having so far avoided the awful ending of Game of Thrones, this is a basic story about friendship, struggle and bravery.

There's no political allegory being rammed down your throat, it's not full of identity politics, it's just a thoroughly entertaining show. There is warmth, decency and friendship without it being cringe inducing and there is buckets of humour without it being jarring or detracting from the story.

The characters are brilliant portrayed by a simply fantastic cast. The two main characters have chemistry that is rarely seen nowadays. But more than that, the supporting characters are also fantastic. Even the extras put in a shift.

The action is exciting without being overdone or overly gory and the scenery, directing, pacing - everything, is spot on.

If you have the time, you could easily binge it in one sitting and you'd still be left wanting more. I'll certainly be watching it all again before much longer.

avis:
A Great Addition to GOT - After Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon, we have a new GOT show in A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms and I have watched all of the 6 episodes, so here is my review for the new show. The premise of the show sees a Hedge Knight, on a quest to truly become a knight when he meets a young squire that will change his life.

Main Character Peter Claffey plays Ser Duncan and he is fantastic in this show. This is the first time I have seen him and he truly encapsulated this role and made me really care about Duncan. He is an interesting character with great development and I really found myself rooting for Duncan, maybe more then any character in this universe.

Supporting Characters Dexter Sol Ansell plays Egg and he is brilliant. He has an extremely bright future and I think this is going to be the start of a great career. Egg is snarky but has plenty of characterisation and the relationship between Duncan & Egg is easily the best part of this show.

Daniel Ings plays Lyonel Baratheon and he provides real energy to this show. Especially over the first few episodes that are a bit slower, he injects life into them and his character is a lot of fun and a real show stealer.

Shaun Thomas plays Raymun Fossoway and he is a great character. He is the ultimate friend for Duncan and he was just a nice character who supported our lead character no matter the circumstances.

Bertie Carvel plays Baelor Targaryen and he is just such a presence on screen. He isn't on the show too much but he owns the show with his presence and is one of the best characters.

Story The story is good, it is much lower stakes then other shows in this franchise but it just works and makes you really care about the characters. The relationship between Duncan and Egg is really well done and the whole concept of the show is really well handled with a pretty satisfying ending.

Script The script is pretty good. It has some really great drama in it that ramps up the issues between some of the characters. There are also some decent humorous scenes which helped Duncan's character. But there is also some humour that really felt out of place and took away from the overall feeling of the show.

Style The style is good, there are some really strong action scenes and it does have the overall feel of Game of Thrones, I just liked the overall vibe of the show. However, the episodes are just too short and to me we could have just got more here and had stronger pacing.

Overall Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a Great show which sets up the stage well for future entries. A few tweaks and it could become just as good as some of the best seasons of Game of Thrones.

Rating - 8/10.

avis:
A Breathtaking Masterpiece - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a triumph that brings a fresh, heartwarming, and deeply human perspective to the world of Westeros. By stepping away from the massive scale of dragons and continental wars, the show finds its true power in the small, intimate moments between a hedge knight and his squire.

The series is built on the incredible chemistry between Peter Claffey as Ser Duncan the Tall and Dexter Sol Ansell as Egg. Watching their bond grow from a chance meeting at an inn to a partnership built on genuine respect and honor is the heart of the show. Dunk's simple but unwavering integrity is a breath of fresh air, making him one of the most likable characters in the entire franchise.

Visually, the show is stunning, using natural landscapes and practical sets to create a grounded, immersive version of the Reach. The action, while smaller in scale, carries immense weight because we are so invested in the characters involved. From the colorful chaos of the Ashford tournament to the visceral intensity of the Trial of Seven, every moment feels earned and impactful.

This season is a rare gem that balances the grit of the Game of Thrones world with a sense of hope and adventure. It is a breathtaking 9/10 journey that honors the spirit of George R. R. Martin's novellas perfectly. I am already counting down the days until we get to see Dunk and Egg continue their travels.

avis:
Oak and Iron, Guard Me Well - I didn't know much about this series when I started watching it, but I still had high expectations. Partly because it has a very high rating on IMDb, partly because one of the episodes even had a 10/10 rating for a while. And of course, it's a Game of Thrones spinoff. Overall, I thought the series was good, but I expected a bit more.

The story isn't as grand as in Game of Thrones or House of the Dragon. It's a fairly simple story, and that might be why I had a hard time getting into it at first. It's basically about a man who is going to participate in a tournament, and that's pretty much it. It wasn't until around episode four that I really started to like the series. Until then, it felt a bit slow. The characters are good and so is the dialogue, but it's hard to truly connect with them when there are so few episodes and they're relatively short. I also feel like the series lacks a clear villain.

That said, the series is well written and well directed. The action scenes are well choreographed, and the makeup work is very impressive. Episode 5 is the one that previously had a 10/10 rating before some Breaking Bad fans started review-bombing it. While I think it's wrong to review-bomb an episode just because you want Breaking Bad to be the only show with a 10/10 episode, I also don't think episode 5 quite reaches that level. Personally, I would give it a 9/10. For it to reach a full 10/10, I think the episode would have needed a longer runtime, or the series in general could have benefited from longer episodes to build up the story and characters more. That said, it's still a very strong episode where we learn more about Dunk's upbringing and background. The episode's message is about never giving up, which I think is very nice.

Overall, it's a very good first season that has somewhat of an old-school Game of Thrones feel to it. I just wish it had been longer. However, more seasons are on the way, and it's always difficult to review and rate something that isn't finished yet.

I've heard that people who have read the book consider it one of the best adaptations, but I can't really comment on that since I haven't read the book myself. Maybe that's part of the reason why some people think the show is better than I do.

avis:
Epic, Intimate and Really Enjoyable - "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" proves that you don't need dragons, massive armies, or world-ending stakes to tell a compelling story in Westeros. This series chooses a smaller, more personal scale, and that's exactly where its strength lies.

The tone is grounded and character-driven, focusing on honor, loyalty, and the quiet weight of knighthood. The relationship at the center of the story carries the narrative with warmth and nuance, offering a refreshing contrast to the political brutality we're used to in this universe. There's a sincerity here that feels almost old-fashioned, in a good way.

The performances are strong across the board, with a natural chemistry that makes the journey engaging from start to finish. The writing is sharp without being overly dramatic, allowing humor and humanity to breathe between moments of tension.

Visually, it maintains the high production value expected from the franchise, though it wisely prioritizes atmosphere over spectacle. The pacing is measured but never dull, giving the characters room to grow.

It may not have the explosive intensity of its predecessors, but its focus and heart make it stand out. A thoughtful, well-crafted addition to the world of cinematic ASOIAF.

avis:
Decent but a Bit Meandering - I've heard nothing but good things about Knight of the Seven Kingdoms. Even my favorite YouTube movie critic, The Critical Drinker, raved about it. But boy, I gotta say, I was bored by this show. I binged all 6 episodes last night because I was told it gets better. The pace of the show is glacial and the characters, other than Dunk and Egg, are hardly fleshed out at all. Most are just cardboard cutouts. There is no character arc from episodes 1 to 6. The villains are evil and the heroes are good. No one has any depth. And boy, could this show use some nudity. There is none, except for a very gratuitous scene of the master night urinating. When I say he is hung like a horse, I am not exaggerating. I miss the political intrigue of the original show. The episodes are just over 30 minutes long, but feel like they are 20 minutes, which is odd considering the slow pace. The writers seem to have a very intense infatuation wit bodily functions.

My biggest gripe however is that this is a really poor knockoff of A Knight's Tale. Poor page dons the armor of his deceased master knight, travels to a jousting tournament and picks up compadres along the way while running afoul of the main villain.

Having said that, the characters of Dunk and Egg are interesting and the by-play between them is funny and heartwarming. The action at the jousting tournament is top notch, brutal and graphic. Body parts and blood are everywhere, but its filmed in a way that is hard to tell who is doing what to whom.

This show has an 8.8 rating on here so maybe I am just being unkind. I have seen much better shows about knights. It has exciting moments, but none of the characters outside of the two leads are memorable or interesting. In the final fight between 14 knights, I didn't feel any dread about someone dying. There was no investment because they didn't take the time to develop anyone or give them interesting arcs. Only Dunk and Egg were developed and even that was pretty limited.

avis:
A Quiet but Powerful Return to Westeros - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms offers something different from the epic chaos of Game of Thrones. Instead of massive wars and political schemes, this series focuses on a smaller, more personal journey through Westeros.

The story follows Ser Duncan the Tall, a humble hedge knight trying to live by the true ideals of knighthood, and his young squire Egg. Their partnership becomes the heart of the series. What makes the show work so well is its simplicity: two travelers moving through a dangerous world, discovering honor, loyalty, and harsh reality along the way.

The writing focuses heavily on character development rather than spectacle. There are no dragons or massive battles dominating the story; instead, the series explores the human side of Westeros and the meaning of being a true knight.

Peter Claffey delivers a strong and believable performance as Dunk, portraying a man who is brave, honest, and sometimes naive. Dexter Sol Ansell's Egg adds intelligence and charm, creating a compelling duo that drives the narrative.

Visually, the show still maintains the high production quality expected from this universe. The costumes, armor, music, and cinematography all bring the medieval world to life beautifully.

The pacing can feel slower compared to other shows in the franchise, but that slower pace allows the characters and themes to breathe. By the end, the series proves that Westeros doesn't always need dragons or massive wars to tell a powerful story.

Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a refreshing addition to the world of Westeros-smaller in scale but rich in character and heart.

Set in the Game of Thrones universe, this series doesn't give priority to power but completely to emotions. This series showcases what Honor means and what common folk life is in the realm. The direction is intentionally intimate, observational, and human-centered, unlike the grand spectacle style of the previous series.

This series has the strongest writing in any of the Westeros' adaptations because it focuses on internal conflicts instead of political conflicts and it showcases that with sheer raw and realism. The acting performances were a masterclass. Each and everyone gave their soul to the roles and they lived like that on screen throughout. Dan Romer peaked with the score. The score was perfect for each sequence. It elevated, intensified and many more. Unlike the epic orchestral dominance of Game of Thrones, this score uses soft strings, ambient tones and sparse instrumentation. This reinforces emotional intimacy. Silence is used brilliantly. The sound design was exceptionally detailed.

Huge Kudos to the production design team and costume design team for their brilliant work. They are the lungs of this world. Without their perfect adaptation, the series won't breathe. The cinematography was magnificent. The wide shots and close-ups were so well differentiated according to the situation. The framings were normal yet the beauty captured was a treat to the naked eye. The lighting was natural. The camera movements were slow throughout but when the tourney arrived, the cinematographer went into peak mode with it. The color palette was dominated by browns, grays, faded greens, cold blues and dull golds. The editing was perfect. No flaws with it. Loved the minimal use of VFX and CGI and full reliance on practical effects just made this show better than House of the Dragon for me.

avis: Hard-boiled Egg. - 'A Knight Of The Seven Kingdoms (2026)' isn't what I expected from a 'Game Of Thrones (2011-2019)' spin-off and is all the better for it. It's smaller, it's gentler, it's more personal and heartfelt, but it's still just as immersive and detailed and character-driven as its bigger brother. While it's the first tale in Westeros to focus primarily on a single character and to take place over just a few days (in addition to the occasional flashback), it's perhaps more distinct for being about a fundamentally good person. Ser 'Dunk' the Tall is flawed, yes, but he lives by a code of honour and always tries to do what's right, standing in stark contrast to the morally grey - often outright despicable - people who not only surround him but also make up the bulk of the cast of 'GOT'. His relationship with Egg, an enigmatic yet endearingly cheeky chappy who wants to be his squire, is well-observed and really quite moving at times. It's also surprisingly funny, something which can be said for the overall show. This is far more comedic than I expected it to be, and it's also stylistically pretty singular - and sometimes straight-up strange - when compared to its more consistently presented predecessors. It makes some bold choices and it's really invigorating to see a spin-off that doesn't feel as though it's confined by the aesthetics and expectations of its source material. This isn't a referential side dish, it's a delicious main course. The first two episodes are quaint and quite slow, but they're exactly what they need to be. The next three become increasingly compelling and occasionally brutal, making good use of the goodwill garnered by the excellent character work earlier on to keep you bolted to the edge of your seat. The finale is expectedly low-key, as 'GOT' finales usually are, and acts as an enjoyable epilogue that sets up a potential second series perfectly. The season is structured more like a movie, and it isn't much longer than one, but it works well for what it is and certainly doesn't outstay its welcome. I could honestly watch a dozen more seasons - as long as they're a similar quality, of course - and I hope that I at least get to see one or two more. I'm not done with Dunk and Egg just yet, and I don't think anybody else is either. This is a fantastic little show that's sometimes slightly mild precisely because that's what's required of it. It isn't epic, but it's quite immense in its own way. I'd even argue that it's greater than the sum of its parts. I like it a lot.

avis:
Great - After finishing the first 5 episodes of A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, I can honestly say it's a solid 10/10 for me.

What makes this show special is that it doesn't try to copy Game of Thrones. It feels more grounded and personal. The story focuses mainly on Dunk and Egg, and that simple dynamic is what carries everything. Dunk isn't some perfect hero - he's rough, sometimes confused, and just trying to live up to the idea of what a true knight should be. That struggle feels real. Egg, on the other hand, is sharp, stubborn, and clearly meant for something bigger. Watching their bond grow across these episodes is easily the best part of the show.

Across the five episodes, the pacing is steady. It builds slowly but never feels boring. The tension increases naturally. The politics are there, but they don't overpower the characters. Every decision feels like it matters. There aren't crazy shocking deaths every episode - instead, it focuses on honor, loyalty, pride, and power.

Visually, the show looks amazing. The armor, castles, tourneys, and countryside all feel authentic. It truly feels like Westeros, but in a more classic, knightly era. The music also adds a lot - subtle but powerful.

What I appreciate most is the heart of the show. It's not about dragons or huge wars. It's about what it means to be a knight, what it means to lead, and how friendship can shape history.

Five episodes in, and I'm fully invested. If it continues like this, it could become one of the strongest stories in the whole Westeros universe.

A Promising Start That Needs Time to Mature - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms has done a great job for its first season. The series manages to capture the spirit of Westeros while telling a smaller and more personal story. However, it still feels like the show needs a bit more time to fully mature.

The pacing is somewhat slow and the story progresses calmly, but it remains engaging. It has that kind of storytelling that makes you say, "Alright, just one more episode." The atmosphere and character interactions keep you invested even when the plot moves at a slower pace.

I'm confident that in a few seasons we'll be watching something truly special. Much of this expectation comes from the potential character development of Egg and Ser Duncan the Tall. As they grow both as characters and in age, the story will likely evolve in exciting ways. I'm especially looking forward to seeing how that journey unfolds over time.

My only real criticism is the episode length. I expected episodes to be at least 45 minutes long, and the shorter runtime sometimes makes the story feel a bit limited. With longer episodes, the world and characters could be explored in greater depth.

Overall, it's a very promising start, and I'm excited to see where the story goes in future seasons.

Got at its best - Here's a ~300-word review written in a passionate, personal tone since you loved it:

---

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a quiet masterpiece-proof that epic fantasy doesn't always need dragons, massive wars, or thrones to be powerful. I absolutely loved this book for its simplicity, heart, and humanity.

Set about a century before the events of Game of Thrones, the story follows Ser Duncan the Tall and his squire, Egg. What makes this book special is how grounded it feels. Dunk isn't a legendary knight-he's awkward, honorable, and often unsure. That imperfection makes him incredibly real. His strong moral compass, even when it gets him into trouble, is what truly defines knighthood in this world.

Egg, on the other hand, is sharp, curious, and quietly fascinating. The dynamic between Dunk and Egg is the soul of the book. Their conversations are warm, funny, and meaningful, slowly building a bond that feels genuine and earned. There's a sense of companionship that stays with you long after you finish reading.

Unlike the grand political chaos of Westeros we're used to, this book focuses on smaller conflicts-tournaments, personal honor, village disputes-but they feel just as impactful. George R. R. Martin's writing shines here: subtle world-building, rich dialogue, and emotional depth without excess brutality.

What I loved most is how this book explores the idea of knighthood. It asks what it truly means to be a knight-not by birth or title, but by choices, kindness, and courage. The stories are calm yet powerful, nostalgic yet meaningful.

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms feels like a warm campfire tale from Westeros-gentler, wiser, and deeply satisfying. For fans of the world, it's not just a side story; it's a reminder of why this universe is so unforgettable.

I know what's the story is about. And even like this, the pacing is off. We have seen 5 filler episodes that were irrelevant and were filled up with unimportant things. Almost all of these episodes contained some sort of important thing, but these all could have been paced much better and the series would have had the chance to be richer. I get it, subjectively for a lot of people, something irrelevant towards the story makes it more romantic for them because it adds more unimportant details for the character.

The lenght of the episodes and the series itself serve 2 purpose.

1. this was a cheaper series, with a lot of risk as it has nothing that would attract the general viewer. (As I stated above, there was one question the series brought up, the fight. Who wins? - and this is not something that would keep the people there in theory. And this is why all the episodes were filled up with this and that, to make it cheap.) 2. Due to the lower budget, they had to stick with a short format. (Now, they will keep it for the second season because they believe this was a major point in the success of the series.)

I would like to highlight that I'm not a "hater". I explained why this series is lacking and why in other aspects it is good. These are all objective matters. Objectively, this is an average 6/10.

Even that 8/10 that the first episode received is incredibly overrated. The last episode was indeed by far the best, yet even with that it is overall just a 6. The episode itself is about a 7.

In my personal, subjective opinion, it had it's points here and there, I can understand the success in this shallow world and I can absolutely understand those that stating the true worth of this series.

The pacing is steady and easy to follow. The tone mixes adventure, humor, and quiet sadness. It shows what knighthood really means, not just fighting but choosing honor even when it is hard.

This series proves that the world of Westeros still has powerful stories to tell without needing massive battles. It is grounded, emotional, and thoughtful.

A great watch for fans of Game of Thrones and for viewers who enjoy character driven stories.

Generally the show is likeable though and the above complaints are really all about why we have to strain our senses to watch a TV show when the screen is 90 percent black for most of the time. By the way, as usual, the background music is around ten times louder than the dialogue so while you can hear that same tonic chord over and over you might struggle to hear the witty quip written there by the screenplay team. Good luck to them. I like the show but I wish I could watch more of it rather than wonder what is happening in that utter darkness. avis:
Lots of potential - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms works so well precisely because it doesn't try to outdo the chaos and spectacle that defined so much of Game of Thrones. It's smaller. Quieter. And honestly, that restraint feels intentional - almost confident.

What really carries the series is the relationship between Dunk and Egg. Their chemistry feels lived-in rather than performed, and there's an easy warmth to their dynamic that makes the world feel less brutal and more human. You believe in their bond. It's not just plot-driven partnership - it's mentorship, awkward loyalty, shared uncertainty. That grounding gives the story heart in a way Westeros doesn't always allow itself to have.

The production design deserves credit too. The world feels textured and immersive without screaming for attention. Nothing feels overblown. Instead of dragons dominating the frame, we get dusty roads, quiet conversations, moments of doubt. The storytelling moves deliberately - sometimes almost cautiously - but that patience gives the emotional beats space to land.

What stands out most is the tone. This isn't about kingdoms rising or collapsing under dragonfire. It's about honor. About loyalty. About a young boy learning what kind of king he might become and a hedge knight figuring out what kind of man he already is. That narrower lens actually deepens Westeros. It reminds us that this world isn't only shaped by thrones and wars - it's shaped by the people walking between them.

If there's a critique worth mentioning, it's the episode length. At times, things feel just a little too compact. Not rushed exactly - just... tight. There are moments where you can sense the story wanting to linger a bit longer, to let certain conversations breathe or conflicts unfold more gradually. With material this strong, you almost wish it had the room of a longer arc - maybe even a feature-length format - simply because the character work could absolutely sustain it.

Still, the series ultimately succeeds at what it sets out to do. It tells a grounded, character-driven story in Westeros that feels sincere, focused, and distinct within the franchise. It doesn't rely on spectacle to matter - and that might be its greatest strength.

Something akin to having sugar-injected, fat-inducing, visually pleasing junk food dangled before you just after starting a sorely needed diet... Dragons everywhere, blonde hair worn by every character. Fortunately interesting plots and character dynamics revealed themselves, hiding flaws and drawing me in to the world.

A knight of Seven Kingdoms left me with a similar distaste: within 30 minutes of episode 1, dragons are seen which I cannot help feel are being used as strategic lures, taking advantage of a strong nostalgia for the original Game of Thrones. Set pieces are small and lack the grand feel that we expect from the universe. The dialect characters use is just challenging enough to comprehend that things go over my head at times.

With that being said, I do understand what the show is going for. The first episodes do NOT give the same structured script that we've experienced in GoT and HoD (core characters far apart whose paths inevitably intertwine in the grand finale many seasons down the road). Rather these early episodes seem to be indicating this will be an epic which focuses on the trials and tribulations of one lone hero (think "The Witcher" or "Oblivion").

Many have taken issue with the on-the-nose humor that sporadically pops up, even falling flat at times. To this I do agree. In my opinion the way it is used however is neither overbearing nor being overused. I like that this is being leaned into more than prior shows and tell me the direction and writing is grounded in unique visions for the shows direction.

This is a different beast than what I expected to see from the Thrones universe. There is great potential here. A few more episodes will be needed before deciding if this is worthy of sticking around for.

avis: Best got show - In an era where modern fantasy often prioritizes sprawling geopolitical maps and an ever-increasing body count, George R. R. Martin's A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms serves as a poignant, masterful reminder that the most resonant stories are often the smallest ones told with the most heart. Set roughly a century before the grim winter of A Game of Thrones, this collection of three novellas-The Hedge Knight, The Sworn Sword, and The Mystery Knight-strips away the icy nihilism of the main series to reveal a Westeros that feels sun-drenched, vibrant, and surprisingly earnest. The brilliance of this collection lies in its central duo: Ser Duncan the Tall, a massive, "thick as a castle wall" hedge knight with no true lineage but a desperate, fumbling desire to be honorable, and his squire Egg, a precocious boy whose hidden identity provides a constant, shimmering tension to their dusty travels. Unlike the high lords of the Great Houses who move armies like chess pieces, Dunk and Egg navigate the world at ground level, dealing with the tangible fallout of drought, local feuds, and the lingering scars of the Blackfyre Rebellion. Martin's prose here is leaner and more rhythmic than in his primary cycle, favoring atmospheric detail and sharp, witty dialogue over encyclopedic world-building, which allows the themes of chivalry and class to breathe naturally. We see the Targaryens not as the distant, mad legends they eventually become, but as a family of complex, flawed individuals grappling with the weight of their own dynasty. It is a rare "prequel" that manages to enhance the original material without ever feeling like a chore or a lore-dump; instead, it offers a refreshing, episodic adventure that explores the quiet tragedy of trying to be a good man in a world that primarily rewards the ruthless. By focusing on the bond between a man who has nothing but his shield and a boy who has everything but freedom, Martin crafts a narrative that is both a classic knight-errant tale and a sophisticated deconstruction of the very myths it celebrates, making it an absolutely essential read for anyone who values character depth over sheer spectacle.

avis:
When you stick with the source material - After so many disappointing shows that have abandoned their source material A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a breath of fresh air. Ira Parker, the showrunner on AKotSK delivers a spectacular example of what can be when the people creating a show understand the author's vision of the story. The material added servers to enhance the show and effectively communicate things in the book that are presented as perception and memories by the main character Ser Duncan the Tall, or Dunk as he is known prior to taking up the sword and embarking on the life of a hedge knight. The show brings back heroic fiction but with a twist that makes Dunk more human and sympathetic than many main characters in fiction.

The quality of the filming is awesome, especially considering the show budget is not as huge as many contemporary fantasy shows. The world Duncan and his squire Egg inhabit is completely believable giving the show an extremely high immersion factor. The jousting alone may well be the best depiction of jousting ever depicted on film. Likewise, the armor is completely believable and combatants actually wear helmets avoiding the movie silliness of a knight running around in full plate armor with his head totally exposed. Well, except for one brief period.

Bottom line, if you are a book reader or a show only person A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms may well be the best fantasy streaming show ever or at least to this point. Hopefully the following seasons will maintain this spectacular beginning.

avis:
A Refreshing and Focused Return to the World of Westeros - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms was a really enjoyable watch. What I liked most about the series is how concise and focused it feels. The episodes aren't overly long and the season itself is fairly compact, which keeps the pacing tight. Because of that, the story keeps moving and each episode delivers something meaningful, whether it's character development, action, or new plot elements.

The dynamic between the main characters is one of the highlights of the show. Their interactions feel natural and entertaining, and the main character in particular is very likable and easy to root for. Their relationship carries much of the emotional weight of the story and makes the journey through Westeros feel personal and engaging.

Another thing I appreciated is the setting in a slightly earlier period of the world. It gives the series some distance from the main storyline we already know, which allows it to stand on its own while still feeling like part of the same universe. It expands the lore without relying too heavily on what came before.

Overall, the show feels like a fresh and well-paced addition to the franchise. It's fun, engaging, and never overstays its welcome. I'm definitely looking forward to seeing how the story continues in the next season.

Set in the rich world of Westeros, this series delivers something rare: a deeply personal journey that feels both intimate and epic at the same time.

The dynamic between Dunk and Egg is the soul of the story. Their bond represents loyalty, growth, and the quiet strength of character. Unlike many power-driven narratives, this series focuses on what it truly means to be noble - not by birth, but by choice.

The storytelling is layered yet simple, emotional yet powerful. Every conversation, every moral dilemma, and every act of courage carries weight. It captures the beauty of medieval chivalry while exposing its harsh realities, creating a balance that feels authentic and meaningful.

Visually, the atmosphere of Westeros remains immersive and grand, but the emotional core is what elevates it. This isn't just another tale set in the Seven Kingdoms - it's a story about integrity, friendship, and the kind of heroism that feels real.

avis:
It's a peak show to watch - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a stripped-down, character-driven return to the political world of Westeros-without the dragons, spectacle, or apocalyptic stakes of Game of Thrones or House of the Dragon. Set decades before those events and adapted from George R. R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas, the series focuses on Ser Duncan the Tall and his unlikely squire, Egg. That smaller scope is exactly its strength.

Instead of constant shock value or large-scale war, the show leans into grounded medieval politics, moral ambiguity, and personal honor. Dunk isn't a mastermind or chosen one; he's an underqualified hedge knight trying to do the right thing in a system built on power and lineage. Egg, sharp and observant, quietly represents the future of a broken dynasty. Their dynamic carries the narrative. If their chemistry works, the show works. If it doesn't, nothing else will save it.

The pacing is slower than modern fantasy blockbusters, but that's intentional. The tension builds through tournaments, oaths, reputation, and class conflict rather than dragons burning cities. It feels more intimate and, at times, more realistic. That said, viewers expecting constant action will be disappointed. This isn't spectacle fantasy; it's political and character drama with swords.

Where it has the potential to surpass its predecessors is tone. If executed faithfully, it can capture the moral complexity that early Game of Thrones mastered before it drifted into rushed storytelling. The writing must stay sharp and resist unnecessary expansion or filler.

Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms has the ingredients to be a thoughtful, tightly written fantasy drama. Its success will depend entirely on disciplined storytelling and strong performances-not scale.

Very good show - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a great show because it feels personal, grounded, and character-driven in a way that makes the world of Westeros even richer. Instead of focusing on massive wars or political chaos, it zooms in on smaller, more human stories - and that's what makes it so powerful.

The relationship between Dunk and Egg is the heart of the show. Their dynamic is warm, layered, and sometimes funny, but also emotional. Dunk's sense of honor and simplicity contrasts beautifully with Egg's intelligence and hidden identity. Watching them travel together makes the world feel intimate instead of overwhelming.

What makes the show special is how it explores chivalry and what it truly means to be a knight. It questions the romantic idea of knighthood and shows that true honor isn't about titles - it's about choices. The conflicts feel smaller than in other Westeros stories, but they're deeply meaningful because they focus on character rather than spectacle.

The atmosphere is also incredible. It still feels like the same universe - the tension, the politics, the danger - but it's quieter and more reflective. That slower pace gives space for dialogue and emotional moments to really matter.

Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms proves that you don't need dragons or massive battles to make a story great. Strong characters, moral dilemmas, and heartfelt relationships are more than enough - and that's why it stands out as such a great show.

Good - Review of A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is an upcoming fantasy series based on the novellas by George R. R. Martin, set in the same world as Game of Thrones. Unlike its predecessor, which focused on large-scale political conflict and brutal power struggles, this story takes a more intimate and character-driven approach. The series follows Ser Duncan the Tall (Dunk), a humble and honorable hedge knight, and his young squire Egg, who secretly has a much greater destiny than he initially reveals.

One of the most refreshing aspects of A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is its tone. While the world remains dangerous and politically complex, the narrative feels more personal and grounded. The relationship between Dunk and Egg forms the emotional core of the story. Their bond develops naturally, mixing humor, loyalty, and moral dilemmas. Dunk is not a typical legendary hero; he is flawed, inexperienced, and sometimes uncertain. This vulnerability makes him relatable and human.

The series also explores themes of honor, class differences, and the true meaning of knighthood. Instead of focusing solely on battles and spectacle, it examines what it means to be good in a world filled with ambition and corruption. The political tension is present but subtle, giving viewers space to connect deeply with the characters.

Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms promises a more character-focused and thoughtful experience within the larger fantasy universe. It offers a slower pace, emotional depth, and a nostalgic return to the rich world-building that fans love, while carving out its own unique identity.

avis:
A Love Letter to Westeros - I've loved ASOIAF for years, but AKOTSK is the first show where I've felt truly immersed in the world of Westeros.

The simple story, intimate POV, and lighthearted tone give the pacing - and the world - room to breathe. Watching Dunk and Egg crack eggs, cheer at tourneys, and dig in the mud during tug-of-war felt more like having a great time at a Ren Fest than watching a GOT prequel. What truly made GRRM's world feel vivid and alive, though, was the production team's superb craftsmanship. Every detail felt tactile and intentional; at Lyonel's feast, I didn't just think, "That's great lighting" - I felt the warmth of the candlelights and the safety and sense of a home it provided Dunk.

Peter Claffey and Dexter Sol Ansell *are* Dunk and Egg. I felt the bond between Dunk and Egg as part of the show's atmosphere, even when they weren't in scene together. There's an organic affection and loyalty in their performances that makes this show feel so wholesome and precious. Dunk's awkwardness and Egg's sharpness create some of the best moments in the series.

The entire cast was perfectly cast, as well. I was surprisingly moved by Sam Spruell's Maekar; he adds a layer of vulnerability and depth to the prince that I didn't particularly feel in the books or graphic novels, so I'm excited to see more of him in Season 2... especially after that post-credit scene.

As this is a non-spoiler review, all I'll say is that Ep. 4 & 5 are peak storytelling (that fog was its own main character) and a testament to why we still need stories about goodness and heroes, no matter how trite they've become. The power of the show - exemplified in those episodes and much like in knighthood - is in its honesty and care for the little things. No dragons needed.

Altogether, this show feels like the long overdue love letter to GRRM and his world of Westeros. The entire team clearly gave this their all, and it paid off brilliantly. I've been playing it on repeat, excited for more, and will probably continue to do so until the next season airs.

There is plenty of action nonetheless but it's well dosed and doesn't take over the extremely good story telling and engaging dialogues. I was glued to my TV for 6 episodes and they just flew by. One episode to go though.

The show is likely produced at a lower budget than its famous sibling but it really does not show. Snsnsn - I went into A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms hoping for a return to the layered political intrigue and moral complexity that made Game of Thrones compelling. Instead, this series feels like a diluted side quest stretched far beyond its narrative weight.

While it's based on the Dunk and Egg novellas by George R. R. Martin, the adaptation struggles to justify its existence. The stakes feel trivial compared to the larger historical arcs of Westeros, and the pacing drags without the payoff of meaningful tension. What might work as a tightly written novella becomes slow and uneventful when expanded for television.

The characters, though charming on paper, lack the gravitas needed to anchor a series. Dunk comes across as bland rather than honorable, and Egg's intrigue never fully materializes into anything narratively substantial. The show leans heavily on nostalgia for the world introduced in House of the Dragon and its predecessor, but offers little innovation or depth of its own.

Visually, it's competent-but competence isn't enough. Without compelling conflict, unpredictable turns, or emotional resonance, it feels like a filler chapter in a universe already oversaturated with spin-offs.

avis:
Back to what made thrones great! - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a straight up return to what made the Game of Thrones universe hit so hard in the first place: people, politics, and proper storytelling. I went in excited, but it still managed to surprise me with how confident it feels. This is not a show trying to flex with spectacle every five minutes. It is a show that backs itself with writing, character work, and atmosphere, and it absolutely delivers.

The biggest win for me is the character development. You actually get time with people. Conversations breathe. Motivations make sense. Relationships build naturally instead of being forced by plot convenience. It has that old Thrones magic where a quiet scene can feel just as tense as a battle because the dialogue is sharp and the performances are doing real heavy lifting.

And honestly, the lack of "look at our budget" CGI is a blessing. It feels grounded. Practical. Human. When something dramatic happens, it lands because you are invested in the characters, not because the screen is exploding. The acting across the board sells the world in a way that is warm, lived in, and oddly comforting, even when the stakes start creeping in.

There is also a real sense of heart here. It has humour, charm, and that cosy fireside vibe at times, which makes the darker edges feel even sharper when they arrive. It feels like coming home to the best parts of Westeros, but with a fresh voice and tighter focus.

For me it is a 10 out of 10. Proper storytelling, proper characters, and a proper return to roots.

. - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a quieter kind of epic. Where Game of Thrones thundered with wars and prophecy, and House of the Dragon burned with dynastic fury, this story feels intimate-almost gentle.

At its heart are two unlikely travelers: a wandering hedge knight and his sharp-eyed squire, moving through a Westeros that feels lived-in rather than legendary. The stakes are smaller, but somehow more human. Honor matters here-not as a grand slogan, but as a daily choice. So does loyalty. So does kindness.

The series trades spectacle for sincerity, and in doing so, it finds a different kind of power. Its battles are fewer, but its silences speak louder. It reminds us that in a world obsessed with thrones, sometimes the most compelling stories belong to those who never expect to sit on one.

avis:
Good knigth - A Breath of Fresh Air in Westeros: Why "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" is a Masterpiece of Restraint For years, the name "Westeros" has been synonymous with grand-scale political intrigue, fire-breathing dragons, and world-ending threats. However, HBO's latest venture, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, proves that the most compelling stories in George R. R. Martin's universe can also be the most intimate. By shifting the focus from the Iron Throne to the dusty roads of the Reach, the series recaptures the heart and soul of the franchise.

At its core, the show is a character study of an unlikely duo: Ser Duncan the Tall (Peter Claffey) and his diminutive squire, Egg (Dexter Sol Ansell). Claffey brings an incredible sense of "noble humility" to Dunk; he is a man who isn't the smartest or the most skilled warrior, but he possesses a moral compass that feels radical in a world defined by cynicism. Opposite him, Ansell's portrayal of Egg is a revelation-balancing a hidden royal heritage with the boisterous curiosity of a child. Their chemistry is the engine that drives the series, making every tavern conversation as gripping as any dragon duel.

Visually, the series is a triumph of "grounded fantasy." Instead of CGI-heavy battles, we are treated to the vibrant pageantry of a medieval tournament at Ashford Meadow. The production design prioritizes historical texture-worn leather, dented armor, and the lived-in mud of a traveling camp-giving the Seven Kingdoms a tangible, gritty reality that feels more immersive than ever.

While some may find the shorter 30-to-40-minute episodes a departure from the usual hour-long HBO epic, this brevity works in the show's favor. It mirrors the focused, episodic nature of the original novellas, ensuring that every scene serves the development of the characters rather than filling a runtime.

Ultimately, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms succeeds because it remembers that chivalry isn't about magic; it's about the choices made when no one is looking. It is a warm, humorous, yet occasionally brutal reminder of why we fell in love with this world in the first place. It is, quite simply, the best adaptation of Martin's work to date.

Review of s1 - A Faithful, Character-Driven Return to Westeros The Knight of the Seven Kingdoms Season 1 is a refreshing and deeply satisfying addition to the world first brought to life in Game of Thrones. Instead of dragons and massive wars, this series focuses on something far more intimate - honor, friendship, and the quiet tensions of a fragile kingdom.

Set decades before the events of Game of Thrones, the story follows Ser Duncan the Tall and his squire, Egg, on a journey that feels both small in scale and rich in meaning. What makes this season stand out is its simplicity. It doesn't rely on spectacle to hold your attention; it relies on strong writing, layered characters, and the ever-present political undercurrents of Westeros.

The chemistry between Dunk and Egg is the heart of the show. Their dynamic brings warmth, humor, and emotional depth, reminding viewers that loyalty and integrity can still exist in a ruthless world. The pacing is deliberate but never dull - every conversation feels purposeful, every tournament moment carries weight.

Visually, the series captures the grounded medieval realism that fans love, with detailed costumes, atmospheric settings, and a tone that feels closer to early Game of Thrones seasons - focused, restrained, and character-driven.

Season 1 proves that Westeros doesn't need dragons to be compelling. It needs well-written characters and meaningful stakes - and this show delivers exactly that.

Solid 10 out 10 for the season 1.

avis: A great series man 💯💯 - I would give A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms a solid 10/10 stars for its charm, storytelling depth, and emotional richness, especially for readers who love character-driven fantasy. Written by George R. R. Martin, this collection of novellas-The Hedge Knight, The Sworn Sword, and The Mystery Knight-serves as a prequel to the epic world of A Song of Ice and Fire, but it feels refreshingly personal and intimate compared to the larger political chaos seen in Game of Thrones. The story follows Ser Duncan the Tall (Dunk), a humble and honorable hedge knight, and his sharp-witted squire Egg, who is secretly Aegon Targaryen. What makes this book outstanding is its focus on ideals of knighthood, loyalty, justice, and friendship rather than just power struggles and shocking twists. Dunk is not the smartest or most strategic character, but his strong moral compass and genuine heart make him incredibly relatable and admirable. The relationship between Dunk and Egg is beautifully written, full of humor, subtle mentorship, and growing mutual respect, which adds warmth to the story. The world-building remains rich and detailed, but it never overwhelms the reader; instead, it provides historical depth that enhances the lore of Westeros without requiring prior knowledge of the main series. The pacing is steady, the dialogue is sharp, and the themes of honor versus reality are thoughtfully explored. Unlike darker fantasy tales that rely heavily on brutality, this book balances realism with hope, making it both engaging and meaningful. Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms stands out as a heartfelt, adventurous, and emotionally satisfying fantasy read that proves Martin can master both grand epics and smaller, character-focused tales with equal brilliance.

A Masterclass in How to Bore an Audience - What a staggering letdown. Game of Thrones set a standard for gripping storytelling, complex characters, and relentless momentum. It juggled multiple parallel storylines-moving from King's Landing to Winterfell to Dorne to Pentos-then skillfully wove them together into something epic and unpredictable. This show seems to have studied that formula carefully... and then rejected every single part of it.

Instead, we're stuck trudging through one thin storyline in one location, as if the writers were afraid the audience might get lost if anything remotely dynamic happened. The pacing is so slow it borders on self-parody. The characters are hollow, the arcs nonexistent, and the plot feels less like a narrative and more like something that accidentally happens between scenes of crude humor.

Rather than tension, intrigue, or emotional investment, we're treated to belching and bodily-function jokes, apparently meant to substitute for actual writing. Where Game of Thrones made me impatient for the next episode, this show made me impatient for the episode to end. What should have been a worthy successor instead feels like an expensive experiment in how long an audience will tolerate boredom. It doesn't subvert expectations-it simply fails to meet them.

avis:
It is, quite simply, BRILLIANT! - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (HBO) HBO's A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is, quite unexpectedly, a triumph of tonal precision. In a television landscape often burdened by excess - excess spectacle, excess solemnity, excess myth-making - this series demonstrates something far rarer: restraint.

Adapted from George R. R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas, the production wisely eschews the operatic scale of Game of Thrones in favor of intimacy. And in doing so, it achieves something arguably more profound. Where Thrones was Shakespearean in its political sprawl, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is Chaucerian - earthy, ironic, deeply human, and acutely aware of the absurdity embedded within systems of power.

The writing is the series' most distinguished asset. It understands that wit need not undercut gravity; rather, it sharpens it. Dialogue carries a wry intelligence reminiscent of medieval romance filtered through modern sensibility. Humor arises organically from character rather than circumstance, and it functions not as relief from violence but as commentary upon it. The world is bloody and gritty - yes - but never gratuitously so. Brutality feels historical rather than performative.

Peter Claffey's Sir Duncan the Tall ("Dunk") anchors the series with remarkable sincerity. His performance resists the temptation toward heroic grandiosity. Instead, he embodies moral bewilderment - a man navigating chivalric ideals in a world that persistently betrays them. There is a quiet vulnerability in his physicality, a sense that Dunk's size is both armor and burden. Claffey allows pauses to breathe; he trusts stillness. In an era of overwrought fantasy acting, this restraint feels almost radical.

Visually, the production design leans toward lived-in realism. Armor is dented. Cloaks are weathered. Mud remains mud. The cinematography favors natural light and grounded composition, reinforcing the narrative's human scale. One senses not a mythic kingdom, but a precarious feudal society held together by fragile codes of honor.

Perhaps most impressive is the show's tonal equilibrium. It is witty without flippancy, serious without self-importance, and violent without indulgence. It captures the paradox at the heart of Martin's universe: that heroism is often accidental, that nobility is flawed, and that power structures are sustained by illusion as much as steel.

In short, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms succeeds because it understands that epic storytelling need not always be epic in scale. Sometimes, the most compelling drama lies not in thrones or dragons, but in the moral education of a single man trying, imperfectly, to do what is right.

It is, quite simply, brilliant.

The production values are magnificent; the scenery, costumes, and the general grittiness of the setting feel authentic, as you would expect with such a high-budget production.

It is obviously too early to give a definitive verdict on the whole season, but having read the book years ago, I already know the story is good. The narrative is much less convoluted than the main books, which makes it easy to stick to the simple and fun plot. What I've seen so far stays close to the text, which is always a good sign for long-time fans. If they maintain this level of quality and focus on the character dynamics, this should be a major hit with the original Game of Thrones fanbase. It's the most "at home" I've felt in Westeros for a long time.

Instead of focusing on power struggles, the series tells a more personal and character-driven story, which makes it surprisingly refreshing and emotionally engaging.

Their relationship brings warmth, humor, and sincerity to the narrative, making every episode enjoyable and easy to connect with. It reminds viewers that heroism is not always about greatness or power, but about kindness and doing the right thing even in difficult situations.

The pacing of the series is balanced, allowing the story to breathe and giving enough time for character development. The performances feel natural and believable, helping the audience become invested in the characters' journey. Visually, the show maintains the rich medieval atmosphere fans expect from Westeros, while presenting a softer and more intimate tone that sets it apart from previous adaptations.

What stands out most is how the series captures the human side of this fantasy world. Small conversations, moral choices, and simple adventures carry emotional weight, proving that compelling storytelling does not always need massive action sequences. This grounded approach makes the story feel authentic and memorable.

Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a beautifully crafted series that successfully expands the Westeros universe while offering a fresh perspective. It is charming, heartfelt, and deeply enjoyable - a must-watch for longtime fans as well as newcomers who appreciate strong storytelling and meaningful characters.

A Masterpiece. Even Stronger Than Four Seasons of GOT - The Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is nothing short of exceptional. Where Game of Thrones relied on spectacle, scale, and political chaos, this series thrives on intimacy, character depth, and razor-sharp storytelling.

This is Westeros at its purest.

The writing is tighter. The pacing is deliberate but never slow. Every dialogue exchange feels meaningful. Instead of massive battles and endless power struggles, we get something arguably more powerful: humanity. Honor. Loyalty. Quiet tension that builds without needing dragons every five minutes.

Dunk and Egg are instantly compelling. Their dynamic carries emotional weight that rivals - and in many ways surpasses - entire arcs from early Game of Thrones. The series proves that you don't need sprawling wars to create greatness. You need well-written characters and restraint.

Visually, it maintains the cinematic quality we expect from HBO, but the real strength lies in tone. It feels grounded. Focused. Mature. There's no rush to shock the audience - only to immerse them.

In fact, this single season delivers more narrative consistency and emotional coherence than at least four seasons of Game of Thrones. It reminds us why we fell in love with this universe in the first place.

If this is the standard going forward, Westeros is in very good hands.

A flawless 10/10.

avis:
Finally, a Westeros Show You Don't Need a PhD to Enjoy - Okay so hear me out. What if a Game of Thrones show was actually... fun? Not fun in a guilty pleasure way, but genuinely warm, well-crafted, and easy to get into? Because that's exactly what A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms pulled off, and I think it deserves way more conversation than it's getting.

Created by Ira Parker and George R. R. Martin, the series is the third entry in the Game of Thrones franchise, premiering on HBO on January 18, 2026, and running for six episodes. It's based on Martin's novella The Tales of Dunk and Egg, and unlike its predecessors, it's not trying to be an epic. That restraint is exactly what makes it work.

What's It About?

The show follows Duncan "Dunk" the Tall (Peter Claffey), an awkward man who desperately wants to become a knight. Alone after the death of his mentor, he decides to enter a tournament as a way to make money and prove himself. Along the way, he ends up with a travel companion: Egg (Dexter Sol Ansell), a mysterious bald kid who refuses to leave his side. Egg is resourceful and worldly-wise far beyond his years and doesn't quite share Dunk's bumbling naivety.

The story is set after House of the Dragon and before Game of Thrones, at a time when the Targaryens still hold the Iron Throne but all the dragons are already gone. No white walkers, no massive wars. Just two guys on the road, trying to survive.

What Works and What Doesn't?

The biggest strength here is actually the simplicity. Where Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon were packed with lore, family trees, and political webs you basically needed a wiki to follow, this show requires zero prior knowledge. And that's not a knock on complexity. It's a genuine creative choice that pays off, because it forces the story to earn your attention through character rather than mythology.

Dunk is written as someone who keeps choosing what's right over what's smart, and watching that play out across six episodes gives the show its actual spine. It's not just a "nice guy tries hard" arc. His decisions have real consequences, and the show doesn't let him off the hook for them. That's what separates it from feeling like comfort TV with no stakes.

The chemistry between Claffey and Ansell also carries a lot of weight. Their pairing is what makes the whole show sing, and I'd agree with that. Scenes that could've been slow or expository become genuinely watchable just because of how these two interact.

The show also shifts tone deliberately, with the first half feeling lighter and adventurous before the back half gets noticeably darker. It's a structure that works, though it does mean the early episodes can feel a little too breezy before the story finds its footing.

The clearest weakness? Female characters are largely limited to love interests or sex workers, who end up as plot devices to push Dunk forward rather than fully realized people. For a show that feels fresh in so many other ways, that's a frustrating pattern that's hard to ignore by the third or fourth time it happens.

Who's It For?

This one works well for two very different audiences. If you're already a Game of Thrones fan, it offers a quieter, more grounded corner of a world you know. If you've never watched any of it and always found the franchise too dense or too brutal.

It's not a perfect show, and the writing does let certain characters down. But as a six-episode story about one man trying to do the right thing in a world that rarely rewards it, it lands more often than it misses.

I'll give it a solid 9/10 ⭐

avis:
A Perfect Return to Westeros - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a remarkable achievement and a triumphant return to the world of Westeros. Rather than focusing on massive wars or sprawling political intrigue, the series succeeds by telling a smaller, more personal story filled with heart, humor, and quiet heroism. This grounded approach gives the show a unique identity while still capturing everything that made the setting so compelling.

At its core, the series explores what knighthood truly means. Honor, loyalty, and compassion are treated not as grand ideals but as difficult choices made by flawed people. The storytelling is thoughtful and character-driven, allowing relationships and personalities to develop naturally. The slower pace works in the show's favor, creating a sense of intimacy that draws viewers into the journey.

The performances are outstanding throughout. The central characters feel genuine and relatable, and their interactions bring warmth and humanity to a world often defined by hardship. Moments of humor and friendship balance the harsher realities, making the emotional impact even stronger.

Visually, the series is beautifully crafted. Costumes and locations feel authentic and lived-in, and the cinematography captures both the beauty and roughness of the setting. Instead of relying on spectacle, the show focuses on atmosphere and detail, which makes the world feel real and immersive.

Perhaps the greatest strength of A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is its consistency. Every episode contributes meaningfully to the overall story, maintaining a steady tone and clear sense of purpose.

Overall, this is a near-perfect fantasy series. It combines strong writing, memorable characters, and rich world-building into a deeply satisfying experience. A must-watch for both longtime fans and newcomers alike.

avis:
No that good - I wanted to love this. I really did. But after sitting through what felt like an eternity disguised as an evening of entertainment, I left feeling cheated, bored, and mildly insulted.

The concept had potential - a sprawling, Game of Thrones-inspired immersive experience promising intrigue, drama, and spectacle across seven distinct "kingdoms." What it delivered instead was seven distinct disappointments, each one somehow worse than the last.

"Ambitious" is a Generous Word The production design looked like it was assembled on a Tuesday afternoon with a budget scraped together from a medieval-themed birthday party. The banners were crooked, the costumes looked suspiciously like rental Halloween fare, and at least two of the "kingdoms" were separated by nothing more than a velvet rope and wishful thinking.

The Performances The cast appeared to be operating under the impression that shouting equals acting. Every lord, every queen, every mysterious hooded figure delivered their lines with the kind of desperate intensity that suggested they were being graded on volume alone. Subtlety was not invited to this kingdom.

The Story Goes Nowhere For an event billing itself as an immersive narrative experience, surprisingly little actually happens. Characters threaten each other endlessly without consequence. Alliances are formed and broken within minutes for no discernible reason. By the third kingdom, I had completely lost track of who wanted what and, more importantly, stopped caring entirely.

The Audience Interaction At one point an actor grabbed my arm and whispered cryptically, "The raven knows your name." I do not know what this meant. Neither, I suspect, did he.

The Verdict A Night of Seven Kingdoms is the kind of event that mistakes busyness for excitement and noise for drama. It is exhausting without being thrilling, complex without being interesting, and long without being epic.

Save your money. Stay home. Rewatch actual Game of Thrones - even the final season is a more satisfying experience than this.

Best show ever after GOT - Best one yet. I just finished watching Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, and honestly, I didn't expect to love it this much.

Going in, I thought it would just feel like a smaller spin-off set in the world of Game of Thrones - but it turned out to be something much more heartfelt and personal. Instead of massive wars and constant political chaos, this show focuses on two characters: Dunk and Egg. And somehow, that smaller scale makes everything feel more real.

What I loved most was the relationship between them. Dunk isn't a perfect knight - he's rough around the edges, unsure of himself, and constantly trying to live up to an ideal of honor. Watching him struggle with what it truly means to be a knight felt refreshing. Egg, on the other hand, brings intelligence, confidence, and just enough mystery to keep things interesting. Their bond slowly grows in a way that feels natural and earned, not rushed.

Compared to Game of Thrones, this series feels quieter but more emotionally grounded. Game of Thrones was intense - betrayals, shocking deaths, dragons, and large-scale battles. It was epic in every sense. But Knight of the Seven Kingdoms feels more intimate. The stakes are smaller, yet somehow they hit harder because you're deeply invested in the characters rather than the politics of entire kingdoms.

That's not to say the world-building isn't strong. Westeros still feels rich and layered, just like in the universe created by George R. R. Martin. But here, you see it from the ground level - from inns, tournaments, and dusty roads rather than royal courts. It makes the world feel lived-in and human.

Another thing I appreciated was the tone. It still carries the realism and moral complexity that fans expect, but there's a subtle warmth to it. There are moments of humor, quiet reflection, and genuine friendship that Game of Thrones rarely allowed itself.

By the end, I felt strangely attached - not overwhelmed by spectacle, but emotionally satisfied. If Game of Thrones was about power and ambition, Knight of the Seven Kingdoms feels like it's about honor and growth.

I genuinely can't wait for more. It reminded me why I fell in love with this world in the first place - not just for dragons and wars, but for the people living inside it.
